title: Not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
hook: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
tomorrow: your king comes on a donkey

segments.voice: Yesterday, cieled houses and Haggai's warning about wages that leak away. Your line: a bag with holes.

Same city, same year, same half-built temple as yesterday. Haggai told the people to build, and they did. The man in charge is Zerubbabel, the governor, a descendant of the old kings, with a small crew of returned exiles, not much money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing next to the stories of Solomon's temple. Haggai himself asks who is left who saw the first house in its glory, and whether this one looks like nothing beside it. Into that discouragement steps a second prophet, Zechariah. He doesn't bring a budget. He brings a vision.

Zechariah sees a lampstand of solid gold with seven lamps, and on either side, two olive trees that seem to feed oil straight into the lamps. Nobody presses olives, hauls jars or refills anything. The light just keeps burning, fed from a source the lamps don't control. Zechariah asks the angel what it means. The answer, in the King James Bible: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." The word for might can also mean an army, or wealth, or strength. Power is the strength of your own arm. Zerubbabel has neither, and God says that's fine. That's not how this gets built. Then a picture for the governor's problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain." The mountain might be the opposition, or the sheer size of the task. Either way, it flattens. When the last stone goes on, the people will shout grace, grace unto it. A few verses later comes a question: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The little foundation that looked like nothing is not to be despised. Small beginnings count. Some Christians read the vision as a picture of the Holy Spirit, the oil that keeps the lamp burning. Others hear a word for any work that seems too big for the people doing it: churches, families, movements, one person trying to change. The work still needs hands; Zerubbabel still lays the stones. But the light isn't his to manufacture.
screen: `OIL FROM A SOURCE BEYOND THE LAMP.`
then, large: `NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER, BUT BY MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been pushing on hard, a person you're trying to change, a project that won't move, and notice the clench in your jaw, shoulders or stomach. For a few breaths, loosen it: not quitting, since Zerubbabel kept building, just admitting the oil isn't yours to make. If you pray, hand that one thing to God's spirit; if not, simply let your hands open on your lap.
Zerubbabel. The governor with a small crew and a big job, told the mountain before him would become a plain, not by might but by God's spirit.
Your line: grace, grace unto it. Small beginnings count, even when they look like nothing. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians quote Zechariah 4:6 when starting a work that feels too big, such as founding a church or a ministry, and some read the lampstand's oil as a picture of the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: you're Zerubbabel. small crew, little money, hostile neighbors, and a foundation that looks like nothing beside Solomon's. what word does Zechariah bring you?

original.note: Hebrew: might. it can also mean an army, wealth or strength: everything Zerubbabel didn't have.

trapdoor: what you thought: a motivational line about willpower.
what it means: a governor with a tiny crew is told the work will be done by God's spirit, not by armies or strength, and small beginnings count.
what a scholar hears: the word for might also means an army or wealth, and the vision is set in the same year Haggai urged the rebuilding.
recall: one called to speak for God, out loud
so be it; from a Hebrew root for firm

chat.says: What does not by might, nor by power mean for Zerubbabel's building project?
options: Keep laying stones, but the light comes from God's spirit, not his own strength.
Stop working and wait, since God will finish the temple without any hands.
Gather an army first, so no neighbor can stop the work from going on.
chat.meaning: The lamps burn on oil they don't make. Zerubbabel still lays the stones, but it's done by God's spirit, not might or power.

Zerubbabel.meaning: the governor, descended from the old kings, leading the rebuild

Zechariah.meaning: a second prophet who brought the builders a vision

Solomon.meaning: the king remembered for the first, glorious temple

lampstand.meaning: a stand holding several oil lamps, here seven

notes: Ezra 3:12 records the old men weeping at the new foundation (Haggai 2:3 echoes the comparison). Confirm the link to the same rebuilding era.
Zechariah's early visions are dated to 520–519 BC (Zechariah 1:1, 1:7), overlapping Haggai. 'Same year' is approximate; confirm.
Zerubbabel as governor (Haggai 1:1) and descendant of the Davidic kings (1 Chronicles 3:19). Confirm.
How the olive trees supply the lamps is described in 4:12 with golden pipes; simplified to 'feed oil straight into them'. Confirm.
Reading the oil as the Holy Spirit is a common Christian interpretation, presented as one reading.
